newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers start final talks on tax cut bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers start final talks on tax cut bill.

text.p: House and Senate lawmakers Friday began the final stretch toward the first major American tax cut in 16 years, expressing optimism that they could craft a compromise bill President Clinton would sign.
"I can safely say that no one sitting here today will get all that they want," said Sen. William Roth, chairman of the group working out differences between House and Senate plans.
"But when we're through -- when Congress passes this legislation and the president signs it -- Americans will get what they need: real tax relief," the Delaware Republican said.

The lawmakers will try to carve one final tax bill from the different versions passed by the House and Senate, with an eye to objections raised by the White House over provisions in both. They aim to present the legislation to the full House and Senate for a vote before the August recess.
The tax bill would turn into law part of a five-year balanced budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House that called for $85 billion in net tax cuts.
Clinton believed differences would be resolved, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

"I think the president's view is that the spirit of bipartisanship is holding on the Hill and that the likelihood of tax cut legislation and spending legislation that reflects the bipartisan balanced budget agreement is still quite likely," McCurry told reporters in Romania.

"I remain upbeat that what we began two years ago when we first proposed a similar tax relief plan will be shortly signed into law," Representative Bill Archer, a Texas Republican who is vice chairman of the group negotiating the tax bill compromise, said. "I see no reason why we will not get this bill done this year."
Archer and Roth were the chief architects of the respective tax bills passed by the House and Senate. The Senate version drew more bipartisan votes and less fire from the White House.

The issue of "fairness" has dominated the debate. Democrats say the Republican legislation gives too big a share of the tax cuts to the wealthy at the expense of low-income families. Republicans say their plans give the bulk of the tax cuts to the middle class and that Democrats want to give money back to families who do not pay income taxes.
Lawmakers stressed issues they saw as priorities.

Representative Charles Rangel of New York, the ranking Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, focused on education. "It seems to me ... that it's going to take a lot of flexibility in this conference if we are going to overcome the objections the president has," he said.
The White House has said the House and Senate legislation shortchanged the roughly $35 billion agreed upon in the budget agreement for higher education incentives.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, the senior Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said he wanted to make permanent the exclusion from income of employer-provided educational assistance for graduates and undergraduates. He also wanted to preserve a proposed $2.3 billion funding for the Amtrak rail line.
Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said: "This very small group has a very, very big job."

One issue he wanted addressed was the proposed transfer of the 4.3 cent gasoline tax from the general fund to the transportation trust fund. Spending that money only for transportation could over five years result in $36 billion cuts in other programmes such as education and health, he said.
Lawmakers planned to put compromise offers on the table next week with smaller, less contentious issues expected to be dealt with first, followed by the major sticking points.
Clinton will meet with Republican and Democratic congressional leaders on Capitol Hill Tuesday to discuss the status of the tax and spending cut legislation, McCurry said.
